stem: A case-control study of alcohol use and bladder cancer reports an odds ratio of 3.0 (95% confidence interval 1.4 to 6.4).
oneliner: case-control + OR 3.0 + 95% CI 1.4-6.4 → which interpretation?
ask: Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: Alcohol use is significantly associated with higher odds of bladder cancer
options.B: Alcohol use is proven to cause bladder cancer
options.C: The association between alcohol and bladder cancer is not significant
options.D: The true odds ratio has a 95% probability of being exactly 3.0
options.E: Alcohol use accounts for 3% of all bladder cancer cases

whyNot.B: Association alone does **not prove causation**
whyNot.C: The interval **excludes 1**, so the result is significant
whyNot.D: The interval is a **range of plausible values**, not a probability for one exact value
whyNot.E: An OR does not give the **share of cases attributable** to the exposure; that needs incidence, which a case-control design cannot give

answer: A significant association with higher odds
why: An OR above 1 means **higher odds of exposure among cases**. Because the **95% CI (1.4 to 6.4) does not include 1**, the association is **statistically significant**.

idea.rule: OR > 1 with a CI excluding 1 = significant positive association.
also: CI containing 1 = not significant
OR < 1 with CI excluding 1 = significant protective association
Odds ratio is not relative risk
Wide CI = imprecise estimate

stem: A trial compares two surgical procedures for wound infection. The risk with procedure A relative to procedure B is 0.66 (95% confidence interval 0.30 to 1.45).
oneliner: RR 0.66 + 95% CI 0.30-1.45 → which conclusion?
ask: Which conclusion is best supported?

options.D: Procedure A lowers infection risk by 34%
options.E: No statistically significant difference was demonstrated

whyNot.A: The interval **includes 1**, so superiority is not shown
whyNot.B: The interval **includes 1**, so superiority of B is not shown either; the point estimate even leans toward A
whyNot.C: Nonsignificance means **no difference was shown**, not that equality was proven
whyNot.D: The 34% figure is the **point estimate only**; the interval spans a benefit and a harm

why: For a ratio measure, **1 means no effect**. The 95% CI **0.30 to 1.45 spans 1**, so p > 0.05 and **neither procedure** can be called superior.

idea.rule: Ratio measure whose 95% CI includes 1 = not statistically significant.
also: Difference measure: CI including 0 = not significant
Absence of significance is not proof of equivalence
Small trials give wide CIs
CI and P value agree about significance

stem: Investigators want a quick, inexpensive way to test whether a solvent used decades ago is linked to a rare cancer.
oneliner: rare cancer + exposure decades ago + limited time and money → best design?
ask: Which study design is best?

whyNot.A: A cohort would need **huge numbers followed for years** to see enough rare cases
whyNot.B: Assigning a possibly harmful solvent is **unethical**, and an RCT would be slow and costly
whyNot.D: Cross-sectional gives a **single snapshot** with too few cases of a rare disease
whyNot.E: A case series has **no comparison group** to test a link

why: The outcome has **already occurred**, so cases can be found quickly and compared with controls for **past exposure**. It suits **rare diseases** and is the **fastest, cheapest** analytic design.

idea.rule: Rare disease + past exposure = case-control.
also: Rare exposure = cohort study
Testing a new treatment = RCT
Prevalence = cross-sectional
New rare adverse effect signal = case series

stem: A cancer screening program shows longer survival from diagnosis among screened patients. Investigators want a measure of benefit that is not distorted by earlier detection.
oneliner: screening + longer survival from diagnosis + want unbiased benefit measure → best analysis?
ask: Which analysis is best?

options.A: Compare cancer mortality rates between screened and unscreened groups
options.B: Compare 5-year survival from diagnosis between the groups
options.C: Repeat the study with a much larger sample size
options.D: Enroll only volunteers who ask to be screened
options.E: Compare the number of cancers detected in each group

whyNot.B: This is the **biased measure**: earlier diagnosis lengthens it
whyNot.C: A larger sample **does not remove a systematic bias**
whyNot.D: Volunteers add **selection bias**
whyNot.E: More detected cancers can reflect **overdiagnosis**, not benefit

why: Mortality rate counts **deaths in the whole population**, so moving the diagnosis date earlier cannot change it. It removes **lead-time bias**.

idea.rule: Mortality rate, not survival from diagnosis, avoids lead-time bias.
also: Stage-matched survival also helps
Randomized screening trials use mortality endpoints
Length-time bias also inflates survival
Overdiagnosis inflates detection numbers

stem: A screening test is used for a disease that is fatal if missed but effectively treatable. Five cutpoints on the test's ROC curve are being considered.
oneliner: fatal-if-missed treatable disease + ROC curve with five cutpoints → which cutpoint?
ask: Which cutpoint should be chosen?

options.C: Cutpoint with the highest positive predictive value

whyNot.A: High specificity **misses cases**, unacceptable when missing is fatal
whyNot.B: This gives the **best overall balance**, not the fewest missed cases
whyNot.C: High PPV favors **fewer false positives**, again at the cost of missed cases
whyNot.E: The middle point has no rationale tied to the **cost of a missed case**

why: When a missed case is **fatal** and treatment works, the priority is **no false negatives**. A test with the **highest sensitivity** misses the fewest cases; the extra false positives can be sorted out later.

idea.rule: Dangerous-to-miss disease: maximize sensitivity (rule out). Harmful false positives: maximize specificity (rule in).
also: SNOUT: sensitive test, negative rules out
SPIN: specific test, positive rules in
Lowering the cutoff (high values = disease) raises sensitivity
False positives are then resolved by confirmatory testing

stem: A toxic treatment is planned for children with rotavirus diarrhea, so false-positive diagnoses must be kept as few as possible. Test X has sensitivity 95% and specificity 90%; test Y has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. The errors of the two tests are independent.
oneliner: toxic therapy + must minimize false positives + test X (sens 95%, spec 90%) and test Y (sens 90%, spec 95%) → best strategy?
ask: Which testing strategy gives the fewest false-positive diagnoses?

options.B: Treat only children positive on test X and then on test Y
options.D: Treat children positive on either test X or test Y
options.E: Use test X, and retest with Y only if X is negative

whyNot.A: Test Y alone has specificity **95%**; requiring both tests raises it to **99.5%**
whyNot.C: Test X alone has the **lower specificity (90%)**, so it gives the most false positives of the single tests
whyNot.D: 'Either positive' (parallel) **raises sensitivity** but lowers specificity to 0.90 × 0.95 = 85.5%
whyNot.E: Treating X-negative children who are Y-positive **adds positives**; this is parallel testing and lowers specificity

answer: Serial testing: treat only if both tests are positive
why: A false positive must now fool **both** tests: combined specificity = 1 − (0.10 × 0.05) = 1 − 0.005 = **99.5%**, higher than either test alone (90% or 95%). The price is lower sensitivity: 0.95 × 0.90 = **85.5%**.

idea.rule: Serial testing raises specificity and PPV; parallel testing raises sensitivity and NPV.
also: Parallel testing (either positive) raises sensitivity and NPV
Screen with a sensitive test, then confirm with a specific one
HIV: antigen/antibody immunoassay first, then HIV-1/2 differentiation assay
Serial sensitivity = product of the two sensitivities

stem: Investigators compare the mean serum cholesterol (mg/dL) of 150 coffee drinkers with that of 150 nondrinkers.
oneliner: mean cholesterol + two independent groups → which test?
ask: Which statistical test is most appropriate?

whyNot.B: Chi-square compares **proportions** (categorical data)
whyNot.C: ANOVA is for **three or more groups**
whyNot.D: Correlation measures a **relationship between two continuous variables** in one sample, not a group comparison
whyNot.E: Fisher exact is a **categorical** test for small counts

why: The outcome is a **continuous variable** compared between **two independent groups**, which calls for a **t-test**. Three or more groups would need ANOVA.

idea.rule: Means: 2 groups = t-test, 3+ groups = ANOVA; proportions = chi-square.
also: Paired t-test: same subjects measured twice
Chi-square: proportions across groups
Fisher exact: small categorical counts
Pearson: relationship between two continuous variables

stem: Two towns record the same number of new cases per 1,000 residents each year of a chronic disease. A survey of both towns on the same day finds that the proportion of residents currently living with the disease is twice as high in town B.
oneliner: Same yearly incidence in two towns + point prevalence ×2 in town B → ? → ?
ask: Which explanation best fits these findings?

options.A: A higher case fatality in town B
options.B: A longer average duration of disease in town B
options.C: More new cases each year in town B
options.D: Heavier use of health care in town B
options.E: More asymptomatic cases in town B

whyNot.A: Early death **shortens** duration and would **lower** prevalence in town B, the opposite of what is seen
whyNot.C: Incidence is **stated to be equal**, so new cases cannot explain the gap
whyNot.D: Use of care does not change how many people **have** the disease when incidence is equal
whyNot.E: Asymptomatic cases are still cases counted in **both** towns' incidence; they do not widen the gap

answer: Longer disease duration in town B
why: Prevalence ≈ **incidence × duration**. With **equal incidence**, a prevalence twice as high means people stay in the prevalent pool about **twice as long**. Higher case fatality or faster cure would shorten duration and lower prevalence.

idea.rule: Prevalence = incidence × mean duration (P ≈ I × D).
also: Effective treatment that prolongs life without curing raises prevalence
A cure or high case fatality lowers prevalence
A short illness like influenza has high incidence but low prevalence
Diabetes prevalence rises as insulin extends survival

stem: A health department wants to know what proportion of adults in a city currently have depression. It does not need to follow anyone over time.
oneliner: City wants current proportion of adults with depression, no follow-up → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is best suited to this aim?

whyNot.A: A cohort measures **incidence** over time, which is not needed
whyNot.B: A case-control study starts from **cases and controls**, so it cannot give a population proportion
whyNot.C: Nothing is being **assigned**, so no trial
whyNot.E: A case series has **no denominator** to define a proportion

why: The aim is **prevalence**, the current proportion with the condition. A **cross-sectional survey** of a population sample measures this at **one point in time** without follow-up.

idea.rule: Prevalence needs a cross-sectional survey of the population.
also: Estimating the burden of a disease today
Planning health services
Screening surveys
Not suited for rare disease or incidence

stem: Investigators want to measure the incidence of several diseases, and the relative risk for each, in workers exposed to a solvent compared with unexposed workers.
oneliner: Aim: incidence + relative risk of several outcomes after one exposure (solvent) → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is best suited to this aim?

whyNot.B: A case-control study starts with **one disease** and cannot give incidence or relative risk
whyNot.C: A cross-sectional study gives **prevalence**, not incidence
whyNot.D: A case series has **no comparison group**
whyNot.E: Ecological data lack **individual exposure** information

why: Following **exposed and unexposed groups forward** gives **incidence** and **relative risk**, and can look at **several outcomes** from a single exposure. This is a **cohort study**.

idea.rule: One exposure, many outcomes, incidence and RR = cohort.
also: Framingham Heart Study
Nurses' Health Study
Occupational exposure studies
Prospective or retrospective designs

stem: A company wants the strongest evidence from a single study that its new statin reduces the rate of myocardial infarction. Assigning patients to the drug or a comparator is ethical.
oneliner: Aim: strongest single-study proof a new statin lowers MI, assignment ethical → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is best suited to this aim?

whyNot.A: Cohorts are open to **confounding** because exposure is not assigned
whyNot.B: A case-control study is vulnerable to **recall and selection bias**
whyNot.D: A cross-sectional study cannot show **temporal sequence**
whyNot.E: Ecological data cannot show **individual-level effects**

why: **Randomization** balances **known and unknown confounders** between groups, so an RCT gives the best single-study evidence of **causal benefit** when assignment is ethical.

idea.rule: Randomization is what supports causal inference.
also: Allocation concealment and blinding reduce bias
Intention-to-treat preserves randomization
Not ethical for harmful exposures such as smoking
Gold standard for testing interventions

stem: A planned trial will give each migraine patient drug A for 4 weeks and then drug B for 4 weeks, counting headache days in each period. The investigators worry that the first drug's effect could influence the second period.
oneliner: Each migraine patient gets drug A then drug B; worry about carryover → ? → ?
ask: Which design feature is needed to address this concern?

whyNot.B: Stratification balances **baseline factors**, not residual drug effect
whyNot.C: A run-in selects participants but does not **clear drug A**
whyNot.D: ITT keeps patients in their **assigned group** for analysis; it does not remove carryover

why: In a **crossover trial** each subject receives **both treatments** in sequence, so the first drug may **carry over**. A **washout period** lets its effect disappear before the second begins.

idea.rule: Crossover design needs a washout to prevent carryover.
also: Each patient serves as their own control
Needs stable, chronic conditions
Not suitable for curative treatments
Order of treatments is randomized

stem: A report describes 8 patients who each developed a rash within two weeks of starting a new antiepileptic drug. The report contains no comparison group.
oneliner: Report of 8 patients with rash after a new antiepileptic, no controls → ? → ?
ask: Which conclusion is supported by this report?

options.A: The drug is proven to cause the rash
options.B: A link is possible and worth further study
options.C: The relative risk of rash can be calculated
options.D: The incidence of rash on this drug can be estimated
options.E: The drug is safe apart from the rash

whyNot.A: Without a comparison group, **causation cannot be shown**
whyNot.C: Relative risk needs **exposed and unexposed** groups
whyNot.D: Incidence needs a **denominator** of all treated patients
whyNot.E: With **no comparison group** and only 8 patients, the report cannot establish safety

why: A **case series** describes patients **without a comparison group**, so it cannot show association, risk, or causation. Its role is to **describe** and **generate hypotheses**.

idea.rule: No control group means description and hypothesis only.
also: Early reports of a new syndrome
Initial AIDS cases in 1981
Rare drug reactions
Basis for later case-control or cohort studies

stem: A study finds that countries with more televisions per household have higher diabetes rates. Only national averages were available, with no individual-level data.
oneliner: Countries with more TVs per household have more diabetes; national averages only → ? → ?
ask: Which conclusion is valid?

options.A: The link holds for countries but may not for individuals
options.B: Individuals who own a TV are more likely to develop diabetes
options.C: Television ownership is a cause of diabetes
options.D: The relative risk for TV owners can be calculated
options.E: The diabetes risk of each household is known

whyNot.B: That applies a group finding to **individuals**, the ecological fallacy
whyNot.C: Correlation across countries does not prove **causation**
whyNot.D: Relative risk needs **individual exposure data**, which are missing
whyNot.E: Only **averages** were studied, not households

why: Ecological data describe **populations**, so the association holds for **countries** and not necessarily for **individuals**. Inferring individual risk is the **ecological fallacy**.

idea.rule: Ecological associations cannot be applied to individuals.
also: Countries with high fat intake have more colon cancer
Cities with more doctors have more deaths
Confounding by country-level factors
Group averages hide individual variation

stem: A physician wants the strongest available evidence about a drug for heart failure. Several well-conducted randomized trials have already been published.
oneliner: Best evidence for a heart-failure drug, several good RCTs published → ? → ?
ask: Which source gives the strongest evidence?

whyNot.A: A cohort study is **not randomized** and is open to confounding
whyNot.B: A case-control study is open to **recall and selection bias**
whyNot.C: Expert opinion is the **weakest** level of evidence
whyNot.E: A case series has **no comparison group**

why: A **meta-analysis** of **well-done RCTs** sits at the top of the hierarchy of evidence because it **pools** randomized data. It is still **limited by the quality** of the included studies.

idea.rule: Meta-analysis of good RCTs is the highest level of evidence.
also: RCT ranks above cohort and case-control
Cohort ranks above case-control
Case series and opinion rank lowest
Poor primary studies limit a meta-analysis

stem: A physician wants a test whose negative result will safely exclude pulmonary embolism in a low-risk patient.
oneliner: Need test whose negative result excludes pulmonary embolism → ? → ?
ask: Which characteristic is most important for this test?

whyNot.A: High specificity helps **confirm** disease, not exclude it
whyNot.B: PPV describes a **positive** result, and it is low in a **low-risk** patient
whyNot.D: A high positive LR helps **rule in** disease
whyNot.E: Cost has **no bearing** on how reliably a negative excludes disease

why: To **rule out** disease, a test must have **few false negatives**, which means **high sensitivity** (SnNout). A high-specificity test helps **rule in** (SpPin).

idea.rule: High sensitivity rules out (SnNout); high specificity rules in (SpPin).
also: D-dimer for pulmonary embolism
Screening tests are made sensitive
Confirmatory tests are made specific
A fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody immunoassay is the sensitive screen

stem: A physician compares five tests for appendicitis. Their positive likelihood ratios are 1, 1.5, 3, 6 and 12, and the pretest probability is the same for each.
oneliner: Five appendicitis tests with LR+ 1, 1.5, 3, 6 and 12, same pretest probability → which positive result moves probability most?
ask: Which test's positive result raises the probability of appendicitis the most?

whyNot.A: An LR of **1 leaves probability unchanged**; the test is useless
whyNot.B: **1.5 is a small shift**, closest to 1 after the useless test
whyNot.D: **6 is a moderate rise**, half the size of the strongest test listed
whyNot.E: **3 is a modest rise**, well below the strongest test

why: The further a likelihood ratio lies from **1**, the more it moves the post-test probability. An **LR+ above 10** is large enough to **rule in** disease, so 12 is the strongest of these.

idea.rule: The further a likelihood ratio is from 1, the more it changes probability.
also: LR+ > 10 rules in
LR- < 0.1 rules out
LR = 1 gives no information
LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity)

stem: In a 5-year randomized cancer trial, a participant moves away after 2 years and her status is unknown afterward. The team is preparing the survival analysis.
oneliner: Trial participant moves away at 2 years, status unknown → how is she handled in the survival analysis?
ask: How should this participant be handled in the survival analysis?

options.B: Count her as alive at 5 years
options.D: Exclude her from the whole analysis
options.E: Replace her with a new participant

whyNot.A: Her **death is not known**, so counting it would bias survival down
whyNot.B: Her survival after 2 years is **unknown**, so assuming it would bias survival up
whyNot.D: Dropping her loses the **2 years of follow-up** that are known
whyNot.E: Replacement would **break the randomized sample**

why: She contributed information until **2 years**, then her status became **unknown**. She is **censored** at her last contact, so she counts in the at-risk group until then and not afterward.

idea.rule: A patient lost to follow-up is censored at the last known contact.
also: Censoring also applies to patients alive at study end
Kaplan-Meier uses censored data up to the censoring time
Many dropouts can bias results if related to outcome

stem: In a cohort study, regular exercisers have a relative risk of 0.6 (95% CI 0.4 to 0.8) for myocardial infarction compared with nonexercisers.
oneliner: Cohort RR 0.6 (95% CI 0.4-0.8) for MI in exercisers → correct interpretation?
ask: Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Exercise is linked to a higher MI risk
options.B: Exercise shows no significant MI link
options.C: Exercise is linked to 60% lower MI risk
options.D: Exercisers have an absolute MI risk of 0.6%
options.E: Exercise is linked to 40% lower MI risk

whyNot.A: Risk is raised only if **RR is above 1**; here it is 0.6
whyNot.B: The CI **excludes 1**, so an association is present
whyNot.C: RR 0.6 means exercisers have **60% of the risk** of nonexercisers, i.e. 1 − 0.6 = **40% lower**, not 60% lower
whyNot.D: RR is a **ratio of risks**, not an absolute risk

answer: Exercise is linked to 40% lower MI risk
why: RR **below 1** with a **CI that excludes 1** means the exposure is **protective**. Risk in exercisers is 0.6 times that of nonexercisers, a **40% relative reduction**.

idea.rule: RR < 1 with a CI excluding 1 means a significant protective association.
also: RR > 1 with CI excluding 1 means harm
A CI that includes 1 is not significant
Association in a cohort does not prove causation

stem: An advertisement says a drug cuts fracture risk by 50%. In the trial, fractures occurred in 2% on placebo and 1% on the drug.
oneliner: Ad claims 50% fracture reduction; trial 2% vs 1% → which figure best shows real benefit?
ask: Which figure best conveys the real benefit?

whyNot.A: RRR is the **50% quoted**, and it looks large because baseline risk is low
whyNot.B: RR of 0.5 is the **same relative figure** and hides the small absolute change
whyNot.C: Odds ratio is **also relative**, so it overstates benefit here
whyNot.E: A P value shows **chance, not size of benefit**

why: With a **low baseline risk**, a large relative cut is a **small absolute gain**: ARR = 2% − 1% = **1%**, so **NNT = 100**. Treating 100 people prevents one fracture.

idea.rule: When baseline risk is low, ARR and NNT show benefit that RRR exaggerates.
also: RRR often stays similar across baseline risks
With a constant RRR, ARR rises as baseline risk rises
P value says nothing about effect size

stem: A trial reports a number needed to harm of 50 for hyperkalemia with a new diuretic.
oneliner: NNH of 50 for hyperkalemia with a new diuretic → correct interpretation?
ask: Which interpretation is correct?

whyNot.B: NNH of 50 is **not a percentage**; it equals an excess risk of 1/50 = 2%
whyNot.C: This describes **benefit**, but NNH measures **harm**
whyNot.D: A relative risk of 50 is a **different measure**
whyNot.E: The one in 50 is **harmed**, not helped

why: NNH = 1 / excess risk, so 50 means **excess risk of 2%**. For every **50 treated**, **one extra patient** develops hyperkalemia.

idea.rule: NNH of N means one extra adverse event for every N patients treated.
also: A larger NNH means a safer drug
NNH 50 = attributable risk 2%
NNT and NNH are compared to weigh benefit against harm

stem: A case-control study of drug use in pregnancy and birth defects is being planned. As drafted, each mother would report her past drug use from memory at an interview.
oneliner: Planned case-control of pregnancy drug use and birth defects, exposure reported from memory → best way to reduce the bias?
ask: Which approach best reduces recall bias?

whyNot.B: A larger sample **does not remove systematic bias**
whyNot.C: Hospital controls add **Berkson bias**
whyNot.D: Alpha concerns **type I error**, not bias in exposure data
whyNot.E: Blinding the statistician does not change **mothers reporting from memory**

why: Recall bias comes from exposure reported **from memory**. Using **recorded data** such as pharmacy or medical records, or **prospective** data, removes dependence on memory.

idea.rule: Objective recorded or prospectively gathered exposure data reduce recall bias.
also: Blinding interviewers reduces interviewer bias
Prospective cohorts avoid recall bias
Larger samples reduce random, not systematic, error

stem: In a randomized trial, 20% of patients in the drug arm stopped taking the drug during follow-up.
oneliner: RCT where 20% of drug-arm patients stopped taking the drug → how should they be analyzed?
ask: How should the nonadherent patients be analyzed?

options.B: Move them to the placebo group
options.D: In the group they were randomized to

whyNot.A: Excluding them **breaks randomization** and can bias results
whyNot.B: Moving them to placebo **mixes groups by behavior**, not by random assignment
whyNot.C: Completers-only analysis is **per-protocol**, which loses balance
whyNot.E: New patients were not **randomized**

answer: In the group they were randomized to
why: Analyzing everyone **as randomized**, regardless of adherence, is **intention-to-treat**. It **preserves the balance** of known and unknown confounders created by randomization.

idea.rule: Intention-to-treat keeps patients in their randomized group regardless of adherence.
also: Per-protocol analyzes only adherent patients
ITT is conservative, closer to real-world effect
It preserves randomization

stem: A trial randomizes adults with hypertension to a new drug or placebo. The mean systolic pressure difference (drug minus placebo) is -3 mm Hg, with a 95% confidence interval of -7 to +1 mm Hg.
oneliner: Drug vs placebo + BP difference -3 mm Hg + 95% CI -7 to +1 → conclusion?
ask: Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.A: The drug significantly lowers blood pressure
options.B: The drug significantly raises blood pressure
options.C: The difference is significant because the point estimate is below 0
options.D: The study proves the drug has no effect
options.E: The difference is not statistically significant at the 5% level

whyNot.A: The interval **includes 0**, so a drop cannot be claimed as significant
whyNot.B: Point estimate is negative and the interval **includes 0**; no significant rise either
whyNot.C: The **point estimate alone** does not decide significance; the interval **includes 0**
whyNot.D: A nonsignificant result **does not prove no effect**; the study may be underpowered

why: For a **difference**, the null value is **0**. The 95% interval runs from -7 to +1, so it **includes 0** and the result is not significant at p < 0.05; this does not prove the drug is ineffective.

idea.rule: Differences: null = 0; ratios: null = 1; if the 95% CI includes the null, p > 0.05.
also: Risk difference with CI -2% to +5%: not significant
Relative risk with CI 0.5 to 0.9: significant
Odds ratio with CI 0.8 to 1.6: not significant
A CI that excludes the null corresponds to p < 0.05

stem: Researchers follow 400 smokers and 400 nonsmokers for one year and record whether each person develops a chronic cough (yes or no). They want to test whether the proportion with cough differs between the two groups.
oneliner: 400 smokers vs 400 nonsmokers + cough yes/no → which test?
ask: Which statistical test is most appropriate?

whyNot.B: Compares **means of a continuous variable**; cough here is yes or no
whyNot.C: Compares **means** across three or more groups; the outcome is not continuous
whyNot.D: Measures the **linear relationship of two continuous variables**
whyNot.E: Predicts a **continuous outcome** from predictors; the outcome is categorical

why: The outcome is **categorical (cough or no cough)** and the question is whether **proportions** differ between groups. That calls for the **chi-square test**.

idea.rule: Categorical outcome in groups: chi-square; continuous outcome: t-test (2 groups) or ANOVA (3+).
also: Fisher exact test: same question when expected cell counts are small
Two means, continuous: t-test
Three or more means: ANOVA
Two continuous variables: correlation or regression

stem: A study assigns 90 patients with type 2 diabetes equally to one of three drugs and compares the mean HbA1c after 6 months across the three groups.
oneliner: Mean HbA1c + 3 drug groups + continuous outcome → which test?
ask: Which statistical test is most appropriate?

whyNot.A: Compares **only two means**; there are three groups
whyNot.B: Used for **proportions of a categorical outcome**; HbA1c is continuous
whyNot.C: A categorical test for **small counts**; not for comparing means
whyNot.E: Relates **two continuous variables**; it does not compare group means

why: HbA1c is a **continuous** outcome and there are **three groups**, so the means are compared with **ANOVA**. A t-test would handle only two groups.

idea.rule: Continuous outcome in 3+ groups: ANOVA; in 2 groups: t-test.
also: Two group means: t-test
Proportions in groups: chi-square
Small expected counts: Fisher exact
ANOVA gives an F statistic
